entities.name: Baldus de Ubaldis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Baldus de Ubaldis (c. 1327 – May 7, 1400) stands as the preeminent Italian jurist of the late 14th century, a central pillar in the school of Postglossators, or Commentators, who revitalized Roman Law across Europe. Operating from the vibrant intellectual centers of Perugia, Pisa, Florence, Padua, and Pavia, Baldus synthesized classical Roman legal texts with canon law and feudal customs, providing practical interpretations that profoundly shaped the legal systems of emerging nation-states and the nascent international order. His extensive commentaries on the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, particularly the *Digest* and *Code*, made him a foundational figure whose influence extended from the Holy Roman Empire to the Iberian Peninsula, defining the academic and practical discourse of civil law for centuries.

Baldus commenced his legal education under Bartolus de Saxoferrato at Perugia, receiving his doctorate in civil law at the age of 17 and later in canon law. He held professorships across Italy, including Perugia (1347–1357, 1376–1379), Pisa (1357–1362), Florence (1364–1376), Padua (1379–1390), and Pavia (1390–1400), where he taught until his death. His prolific output comprises over 3,000 *consilia* (legal opinions), extensive commentaries on all parts of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the *Libri Feudorum*, and several works on canon law. He advised Pope Urban VI and was instrumental in shaping the legal arguments surrounding the Western Schism, notably advocating for the validity of Urban VI's election and the deposition of Clement VII.
